findings.title: H1 explains only part of it. The 2022-2025 markdown rise ($4,059,115 on stock lines) is mostly the mixed-refrigerant 2023 cohort, which Hartwell keeps stocking and sells below cost. A real R-410A clearance began in 2025, and its cost arrives mainly in 2026
findings.conclusion: Observed: Every equipment markdown follows one rule, 2.1% a month after the SKU's discontinued_on date, capped at 42% from month 20. A check over every month, cohort and fulfilment type found 0 off-rule lines (q150, q204). The markdown lowers the billed price only on stock lines. Special and transfer lines carry markdown_pct but are invoiced at the unreduced order price, with 0 price differences across 6,354 marked special lines in 2025 (q171, q212). Stock-line markdown went from $1,320,450 in 2022 to $5,379,566 in 2025, up $4,059,115 (q238). The 2023-01-01 cohort accounts for 0.8509 of that rise (q256). That cohort is split evenly across R-410A, R-454B and non-refrigerant SKUs, 44/44/44 (q145), and its 2025 markdown splits the same way: $980,654, $1,069,154 and $1,404,266 (q180). The rise is therefore not an R-410A clearance, and H1 fails as an explanation of 2022-2025. The 2015 and 2023 cohorts carry $4,735,079 of 2025 stock-line markdown. Hartwell stocks them to meet steady demand: 2015-cohort receipts were 2,755 against 2,645 units sold in 2025. The 2023 cohort was phased out in 2023 (823 units returned to vendors) and then restocked in 2024-2025 (q215, q217). Both sell below a buy cost that hasn't changed (q205, q210, q228), for a 2025 stock-line margin of -$2,789,637 (q238). H1 does hold for one cohort: the 129 R-410A SKUs discontinued 2025-01-01 are being cleared. Stock buying fell from 10,326 units in 2024 to 582 (q160), 995 units went back to vendors and on-hand stock fell from 7,099 to 3,442 units (q215, q239). Its markdown is still ramping, at 0.1129 on average in 2025 for $644,487 (q232). Interpretation: R-410A clearance cost grows in 2026. On the 2026 schedule (months 12-23) at 2025's monthly volume, it would be $2,079,237, an average of 0.3643, with margin -$1,128,836. The 3,442 units on hand would carry $2,544,097 of markdown at the 42% cap (q255). Either way, R-410A would be about half of real markdown: 0.5042 on the 2026 schedule (q256), 0.5263 at the cap (q238), against 0.372 in 2025 and 0.3005 in 2022. These are re-pricings of 2025 volume, not forecasts. Action: for the 264 SKUs in the 2015 and 2023 cohorts, decide with purchasing and pricing whether each is really discontinued. Stopping stocking avoids a $2,789,637 yearly loss (q256). Resetting discontinued_on recovers up to $4,735,079 only if volume holds at full price, which these records can't test. For the R-410A cohort, track the 3,442 units still on hand as the markdown deepens.

claims.text: Markdowns appear only on equipment, every year 2016-2025, and were already split across R-410A, R-454B and non-refrigerant SKUs before the refrigerant transition.

markdown_pct = 0.021 x months since discontinued_on for months 1-19, 0.42 from month 20, 0 at month 0 and earlier. 0 off-rule lines in every cohort, band and fulfilment type, sales 2016-2025. It can't vary by channel, order-taker or customer.

Only stock lines are actually discounted. In 2025, price over line cost was 0.7996 on marked stock lines against 1.2013 unmarked, and 1.2002 on marked special lines against 1.2019 unmarked. Invoice price equals order price on every equipment line in 2022 and 2025 (0 differences). So $6,620,818 of 2025 recorded markdown on non-stock lines was never given.

Stock-line markdown: $1,320,450 in 2022, $5,379,566 in 2025, up $4,059,115. The 2023 cohort is 0.8509 of the rise. R-410A share of real markdown: 0.3005 in 2022, 0.372 in 2025 ($2,001,346 of $5,379,566).

2015 cohort: receipts track sales (2,755 against 2,645 in 2025), on-hand stock held at about 1,600-1,760 units, ordered units about 5,600-5,800 a year since 2018. 2023 cohort: phased out in 2023 (receipts 2,013, 823 returned to vendors, on-hand 6,878 to 3,288, ordered 16,108 to 5,757), then restocked (receipts 5,594 and 6,941 in 2024-2025, ordered 9,743 and 10,602). The recovery is the same in all three refrigerant groups. On-hand stock at the end of 2025 was 3,898.

Buy cost is flat. Sales-line cost and PO cost equal product cost (ratio 1.0). Vendor bills average 1.0013-1.0019 of product cost. So below-cost sales are real: 2025 stock-line margin on the 2015 and 2023 cohorts was -$2,789,637, and would be +$1,945,442 at the same volume without the markdown. Vendor credits are small in 2025 ($7,805 and $33,198).

R-410A 2025 cohort: 3,243 stock units in 2025, average markdown 0.1129, $644,487. Volume peaked in months 5-7 at 8.4-12.6% off. Re-priced at the 2026 schedule, the same volume carries $2,079,237 (average 0.3643, margin -$1,128,836). At the 42% cap it carries $2,397,009. The 3,442 units on hand would carry $2,544,097 at 42%, a margin of -$1,535,376. R-410A share on these bases: 0.5042 (2026 schedule) and 0.5263 (cap).

findings.not_evidence_of: Not evidence that anyone priced lines by hand or favoured customers: the rate is identical within each cohort-month. Not evidence that the $6,620,818 on special and transfer lines was given away: invoices show it wasn't. Not evidence that resetting discontinued_on would recover $4,735,079, since demand at full price can't be measured here. The 2026 R-410A figures re-price 2025 volume and are not forecasts. 2026 volume is limited by the 3,442 units on hand and the halt in buying.
findings.could_not_tell: What discontinued_on means to the business, and why the 2015 and 2023 cohorts are still stocked (the 2023 cohort's buying resumed in 2024). Whether volume would hold at full price, and so how much of the $4,735,079 is recoverable. Why markdown_pct doesn't reach the price on special and transfer lines (pricing-rule configuration). How fast the remaining R-410A stock will sell in 2026. Answering these needs product lifecycle records, vendor end-of-life notices, the pricing-rule configuration and 2026 sales.
findings.next_step: List the 264 SKUs in the 2015 and 2023 cohorts from erp_products and review each with purchasing and pricing: stop replenishment, or correct discontinued_on. Ask how markdown_pct is meant to apply on special and transfer lines, and count stock lines only in markdown reporting. Re-run q232 and q239 monthly in 2026 to track the R-410A cohort's markdown and remaining stock.
dead_ends: Comparing markdown rates by channel, taken_by and account manager: moot, because the rate is fixed per SKU-month (q150, q204).
My first claim that the 2023 cohort was 'bought again every year': wrong for 2023, when it was phased out (q215). Restocking resumed in 2024.
Treating the 42% cap as the 2026 R-410A cost: overstated. The 2026 cooling season falls in months 17-19 (0.357-0.399), so the 2026-schedule re-pricing ($2,079,237, q255) is the better scenario.
findings.response_to_challenge: Accepted: (1) The rule and the stock-only discount survive. q204 and q212 confirm them more firmly than the original. (2) The cost caveat falls away: PO, bill and sales-line costs match product cost (q205, q210, q228), so the below-cost margins are real. (3) The 2023 cohort was phased out in 2023 and restocked from 2024, not bought every year (q215, q217). Corrected. (4) $4,735,079 is gross markdown, not recoverable money. dollars_a_year is now the loss avoided by not stocking these cohorts, $2,789,637 (q256, the same value as q238's -2,789,637), with $4,735,079 as the upper bound if demand holds. (5) 'H1 doesn't hold' was too broad. The 2025 R-410A cohort is a real clearance and its cost is still to come. Answered with new queries: the challenger's 42% re-pricing overstates 2026, because the cooling-season months, when most volume sells, fall at months 17-19 in 2026. Re-pricing 2025's monthly volume on the actual 2026 schedule gives $2,079,237 and an R-410A share of 0.5042 (q255, q256), against $2,397,009 and 0.5263 at the cap. The 3,442 units on hand bound 2026 volume: at 42% they would carry $2,544,097 (q255). I keep one part of the original verdict, with evidence: the observed 2022-2025 rise is not an R-410A clearance, since 0.8509 of it is the evenly split 2023 cohort (q256, q145, q180). The revised headline is therefore that H1 fails for the past rise and holds for the 2026 outlook.

findings.title: H3 is not supported as stated. R-410A stock is at a ten-year low, and its 2025 below-cost sales are one case of a company-wide pattern: once any equipment SKU passes its discontinued_on date, stock-fulfilled lines sell below cost and keep getting replenished. Losses on those stock lines averaged $1,689,105.48 a year over 2023-2025
findings.conclusion: Not supported: that Hartwell holds an oversized R-410A stock. Year-end 2025 R-410A equipment stock is 5,601 units ($7,925,627.94 at master cost), the lowest of 2016-2025 (q140). Not supported: that the 2025 margin loss is a refrigerant-transition effect. R-410A stock and transfer lines did lose $458,003.64 in 2025 at 0.9397x cost (q158, q241). But every equipment SKU of any refrigerant, or none, sells from stock below cost once it passes its discontinued_on date: 0.7224-0.8516x after discontinuation against 1.2103-1.2221x before it (q231). Active equipment held about 1.20x in 2025: R-454B 1.2102x and no-refrigerant 1.1995x (q241). Observed, and new here: the below-cost pricing applies only to stock fulfilment. After discontinuation, special-order lines run at 1.1968-1.2113x and transfer lines at 1.2032-1.2183x. Stock lines run at 1.0665x in the first year after discontinuation, then 0.7707x, then 0.7023-0.7027x from the third year on (q259). Stock POs keep replenishing discontinued SKUs: 10,001 units ($11,212,307.23) in 2025 (q235). Size: post-discontinuation stock lines lost $1,689,105.48 a year on average over 2023-2025 (8,940.3 units a year), of which R-410A was $449,213.61 (q261). Interpretation: this looks like a pricing rule tied to the discontinued flag and stock fulfilment, combined with replenishment that ignores the flag. Neither the rule nor the reorder trigger is recorded.

claims.text: R-410A equipment on hand at cut-off: 5,601 units, $7,925,627.94 at master cost. Year-end stock was 9,045 units in 2024 and peaked at 11,366 in 2020. The 2025 level is the lowest of 2016-2025. On hand by discontinuation group: 2015 group 655 units ($816,087.80), 2023 group 1,375 ($1,841,588.18), 2025 group 3,571 ($5,267,951.96).

The R-410A SKUs fall into three discontinuation groups: 44 SKUs discontinued 2015-01-01, 44 discontinued 2023-01-01 and 130 discontinued 2025-01-01. In 2025, stock and transfer lines lost $218,496.24 on the 2015 group and $547,810.66 on the 2023 group. The 2025 group made +$308,303.26 at 1.0646x. The 2015 group has sold from stock and transfer at 0.7159-0.7589x cost every year 2016-2025.

Below-cost selling follows discontinuation, not refrigerant. Stock and transfer lines after discontinued_on run at 0.73x (R-410A, 2015 group), 0.8513x (R-410A, 2023), 0.7413x (R-454B, 2015), 0.8516x (R-454B, 2023), 0.7224x (no refrigerant, 2015) and 0.8438x (no refrigerant, 2023). Before discontinuation, every group runs at 1.2103-1.2221x (2016-2025). In 2025, active R-454B ran at 1.2102x and active no-refrigerant at 1.1995x.

Only stock fulfilment is marked down. For all equipment after discontinuation (2016-2025), special-order lines run at 1.1968-1.2113x and transfer lines at 1.2032-1.2183x. Stock lines run at 1.0665x in year 0 (7,990 units), 0.7707x in year 1 (5,401), 0.7027x in year 2 (7,685) and 0.7023x in year 3 and later (19,393). In 2025, for the same R-410A SKU and quarter, the median stock/special price ratio was 0.8601 in Q2 (165 SKU-quarters) and 0.8078 in Q3 (149).

Below-cost isn't an artifact of stale master cost. Sales-line cost equals master cost on every R-410A line 2022-2025, PO cost equals master in every year 2020-2025, and billed cost runs at 1.0008-1.0015x master on 2022-2025 vendor bills.

Discontinued SKUs keep being bought for stock. Across all equipment, stock POs placed after discontinued_on ran at 1,346-2,698 units a year in 2016-2022, then 4,188 in 2023, 8,929 in 2024 and 10,001 ($11,212,307.23) in 2025. Of 2,967 R-410A stock PO units in 2025, 699 were for the 2015 group, 1,686 for the 2023 group and 582 for the 2025 group.

Sizing, stock lines only, all equipment after discontinued_on: the loss was $408,748.50 in 2023, $2,174,845.71 in 2024 and $2,483,722.23 in 2025. That totals $5,067,316.44 over 2023-2025 on 26,821 units, or $1,689,105.48 a year on average. R-410A accounted for $449,213.61 a year. Pricing these lines at the same year's non-stock price/cost (1.2002-1.2057x) would have given $3,766,723.89 a year more. That is an upper bound, not an estimate, because demand at that price is unobserved.

Returns to vendor against vendor credits: in 2025, R-410A returns to vendor were 1,009 units ($1,476,383.18) and credits $747,413.72. Credits lag returns: 2024 credits were 6.88x 2024 returns because 2023 returns were credited in 2024. Over 2023-2024, 323 R-410A units were returned and 323 credited, at a credit value of 0.8 of returned cost.

findings.not_evidence_of: Not evidence that the R-410A phase-down caused the losses, or that R-410A market prices fell: special-order and transfer prices of the same SKUs held near 1.20x (q208, q224, q259). Not evidence of over-buying R-410A in aggregate (q140). Not evidence that the whole $1,689,105.48 is avoidable. Without restocking, those sales and the customers' goodwill might be lost, and demand at full price for discontinued stock is unobserved. Not evidence about rebates or price protection, which aren't recorded. Not evidence that any person, rep or branch set these prices or placed these POs on purpose: there are no pricing-rule, reorder-trigger or approval records. Interpretation: the year-0 to year-2 deepening (1.0665x to 0.7027x, q259) fits a time-based clearance rule, but the records don't say that.
findings.could_not_tell: What rule sets stock-line prices for discontinued SKUs, and why it doesn't apply to special or transfer lines. Why replenishment keeps placing stock POs for discontinued SKUs. Whether the discontinued_on dates are real: a SKU 'discontinued' in 2015 that is still bought and sold at full price on special orders in 2025 may be a master-data error. Vendor catalogs or the product manager would settle it. Whether the 2025 vendor-credit shortfall will clear in 2026: that needs post-cut-off credits or vendor return terms. Real net cost after any off-bill rebates.
findings.next_step: Pull the pricing configuration that applies to stock lines of SKUs flagged discontinued, and the reorder parameters (min/max, auto-replenish flag) for discontinued SKUs. Start with the 44 R-410A SKUs discontinued 2015-01-01, bought for stock and sold below cost every year since 2016 (q220, q221). Ask the product manager whether those discontinued_on dates are correct. If they are wrong, fixing the master data may remove the markdown. If they are right, stop stock replenishment and route demand to special order, which holds about 1.20x (q259).
dead_ends: 'Stock is large relative to history': no. Year-end 2025 is the lowest of ten years (q140).

'R-410A-specific margin loss of $1,357,642.67 a year' (q173): retracted. The no-refrigerant comparator (q172) was contaminated by the same discontinued-SKU mix. Active SKUs show no shared decline: no-refrigerant equipment went 1.2108x to 1.1995x (q241).
'Price, not mix': retracted. Same-SKU prices fell because the SKUs crossed their discontinuation date and are filled from stock (q220, q259).
'Stock bought in 2025 adds to $7,925,627.94 on hand': wrong wording. That figure is all R-410A on hand, and 2025 stock POs were 2,967 units (q175).
'$728,969.46 unexplained vendor-credit gap': probably mostly credit lag at the cut-off (q244). On 2023-2024 history, about 0.8 of returned value gets credited (q249).
Data concern, not pursued: R-454B SKUs all show available_from 2025-01-01, yet they sold every year 2016-2024 (q124, q127).
Data concern: markdown_pct doesn't describe the price charged. Special-order price/list stayed about 0.83 while recorded 1-markdown fell to 0.6599 in 2025 (q202).
findings.response_to_challenge: Accepted almost all of it. (1) The margin loss is a discontinuation effect, not a refrigerant one: accepted on q231 and q241. (2) My 'R-410A-specific' $1,357,642.67 a year is retracted, because its comparator was contaminated by the same post-discontinuation mix (q241, q245). (3) 'Price, not mix' is retracted. (4) The title wording about stock bought in 2025 is corrected. (5) The vendor-credit gap is reframed as probable lag (q244, q249). (6) Stale cost is ruled out (q197, q199, q227). The challenger confirmed that 'stock not oversized' survives, and it stays. I ran two new queries. The first (q259) sharpens the challenge: the markdown hits only stock-fulfilled lines. Transfer lines of discontinued SKUs hold 1.2032-1.2183x, and the challenger had pooled them with stock. The markdown also deepens with time since discontinuation, from 1.0665x in year 0 to about 0.70x from year 2. That explains why the 2025 R-410A group was still profitable in 2025. The second (q261) re-sizes on stock lines only. The challenger's 'a year' figure ($1,605,222.39, q249) included transfer lines. On stock lines alone, 2023-2025 averaged $1,689,105.48 a year, with R-410A at $449,213.61. I also accepted the point that a finite sell-down isn't an annual figure. The size I use now is the recurring company-wide pattern, which has run every year since 2016 (q235), not a one-time R-410A sell-down.

findings.title: H2 only partly holds: outside markdowns, price-to-list fell about 1 point because low-discount accounts in every cohort stop buying faster, not because accounts were repriced or new accounts signed at bigger discounts. That is $1.43M a year of price erosion on 2025 volume, not a sum retention would recover.
findings.conclusion: Observed: non-markdown price-to-list fell from 0.8442 (2016) to 0.8343 (2025). It declined steadily every year, while the list-weighted price residual stayed flat at 0.98342-0.98387 (q456). Parts, refrigeration and supplies each fell by about 0.9 points (q398). Most of the equipment decline, 0.839 to 0.764, is H1 markdowns (q398). Continuing customers' list-weighted keep (1 - discount) barely moved, 0.8448 to 0.8433 across 1,346 customers (q436), and invoice prices match ERP prices exactly in both years (q446). The decline is a shift in the active customer mix toward higher-discount accounts. Accounts under 10% discount stop ordering faster than others. Of 2016-active accounts, 0.292 of the under-10% tier were still active in 2025, against 0.4802 of the 20%+ tier (q415). The gap holds within every size quartile (q440), every trade (q441) and every branch (q443), and among customers onboarded 2016-2020 (0.5022 vs 0.6483, q451). Lapses are spread evenly across the years (q445). On 2025 non-markdown list value of $140,533,485.01, the mix shift equals $1,428,556.44 of price erosion against the 2016 mix (q449, q462). Of that, $1,080,280.56 (0.7562) comes from 2025 entrants being more discounted per dollar than the 2016 accounts that exited. Interpretation: this happens because low-discount entrants also lapse faster, not because new accounts are signed at higher discounts (cohort averages q404; q451). The $1.43M is a counterfactual on fixed 2025 volume, not money that retention would recover. The larger cost of the churn is probably volume: non-markdown list value fell by $9,502,085.00 from 2016 to 2025 (q456, q462). Its value depends on margin, which the records cannot give. Interpretation: the lever is retention of standard-price accounts. A review of discount grants is not indicated.

claims.text: Price-to-list (shipped qty, list-weighted) falls 2016 to 2025 in categories with no markdown lines: parts 0.8467 to 0.8379, refrigeration 0.8464 to 0.8379, supplies 0.8465 to 0.8373. Non-markdown equipment falls 0.8406 to 0.8281, and total equipment falls 0.839 to 0.764 as markdown lines rise from 3,744 to 18,962.

All non-markdown lines together: price-to-list 0.8442 (2016, 242,753 lines, $150,035,570.01 list) to 0.8343 (2025, 234,834 lines, $140,533,485.01 list). List-weighted keep falls every year, 0.8583 to 0.8479, with no step. The residual price/(list x keep) stays between 0.98342 and 0.98387 in every year.

No repricing is visible in the records. Continuing customers (1,346, active in both 2016 and 2025) have keep 0.8448 vs 0.8433 and price-to-list 0.8308 vs 0.8287. Per customer, the median change is +0.0005. Finance invoice lines match ERP prices on all 246,052 matched 2016 lines and 252,359 matched 2025 lines, with 0 differences. In 2016, customers who later lapsed had the same residual as continuers (ptl/keep 0.8543/0.8683 vs 0.8308/0.8448).

New accounts are not signed at higher discounts. Average discount_pct by onboarding cohort is 0.1355-0.1458 (271-320 customers per cohort), against 0.1412 for 3,154 pre-2016 customers. Discount is essentially unrelated to 2025 volume: correlation 0.0158 for post-2016 customers and 0.0133 for pre-2016 customers.

Low-discount accounts lapse faster. Of the customers active in 2016, the share still ordering in 2025 is 292/1,000 (0.292) for discount under 10%, 337/849 (0.3969) for 10-15%, 368/782 (0.4706) for 15-20% and 352/733 (0.4802) for 20% or more. Lapses are spread across years. For the under-10% tier, last orders fall in 2016: 147, 2017: 123, 2018: 101, down to 2024: 43.

The lapse gradient is not explained by size, trade or branch. Under-10% retention is 0.2763 / 0.291 / 0.3038 / 0.2983 across 2016 size quartiles, vs 0.4916 / 0.4056 / 0.5109 / 0.5132 for 20%+ (173-260 customers per cell). Within trades, under-10% vs 10%+ retention is commercial 0.2609 vs 0.4473, mixed 0.3296 vs 0.4606 and residential 0.2904 vs 0.4431. Under-10% retention is lower in all 12 branches.

The same gradient appears among customers onboarded 2016-2020 who ever ordered. The share active in 2025 is 230/458 (0.5022) for under 10%, 0.5791 for 10-15%, 0.6762 for 15-20% and 212/327 (0.6483) for 20%+.

Decomposition of the keep change 0.8583 to 0.8479 on 2025 non-markdown volume gives $1,428,556.44 in total. Of this, $1,080,280.56 (0.7562) is entrants (2,049 customers, keep 0.8526) replacing exiters (2,016 customers, keep 0.8683). $245,867.49 is the continuers' rising weight (0.4269 to 0.5025 of list), and $102,408.39 is continuers' own change. My original sizing (q418: $1,428,556.45 mix, -$29,882.82 residual rate) agrees to the cent.
Volume context: non-markdown list value fell by $9,502,085.00 between 2016 and 2025. The 2016 exiters' list value exceeded the 2025 entrants' by $16,068,837.46. Continuers grew by $6,566,752.46.

Quote data shows a modest pattern consistent with price sensitivity (2016-01-01 to 2025-12-29). The under-10% tier's quote loss rate is 0.2869, vs 0.275-0.2777 for other tiers. Price is the entered loss reason on 0.5488 of 32,443 lost quotes with a reason, vs 0.5076-0.5191 for other tiers. The only reasons recorded are price and job cancelled.
The mix shift is broad. Line-weighted discount rose 2016 to 2025 in 11 of 12 branches. Toledo was flat (0.142 to 0.1402).

findings.not_evidence_of: Not evidence that reps or managers granted larger discounts, or that new accounts were signed at worse terms: continuers' rates are flat and onboarding discounts are flat. Not evidence that price caused low-discount accounts to leave: the quote loss-reason gap is small, reasons are rep-entered and quote-level, and there are no churn dates or reasons. Not evidence that $1.43M can be won back. It is erosion on fixed 2025 volume, and retention would add volume, not raise price on that volume. Not a margin measure, since cost is a static snapshot. Nothing here points at any individual.
findings.could_not_tell: Whether discount_pct ever changed. Matching ERP and finance prices and a flat residual fit an unchanged discount, but only a discount change log could rule out history being restated in both systems. Why low-discount accounts stop ordering (competitor, closure, consolidation, price) is not recorded. What retained volume would be worth needs customer- or line-level margin with historical cost, which the records lack.
findings.next_step: List lapsed under-10% accounts from all cohorts with their last order day, branch and account-manager rep_id, and have account managers ask whether the account closed, consolidated or moved, and whether price was a factor. Ask IT whether discount_pct changes are logged anywhere. Size the lost volume (not rate) once margin by product line can be estimated. Split the remaining equipment price decline under H1.
dead_ends: New accounts onboarded at higher discount_pct: cohort averages 0.1355-0.1458 vs 0.1412 pre-2016 (q404); discount vs volume corr 0.0158 (q450)
Repricing of existing accounts: continuers' keep 0.8448 to 0.8433 (q436), median change +0.0005 (q413)
Residual drift in the pricing formula: list-weighted residual 0.98342-0.98387 every year (q456)
Size, trade or branch confounding of the lapse gradient (q440, q441, q443)
A single-year event: keep declines every year (q456), lapses spread across years (q445)
findings.response_to_challenge: Accepted all three changes; nothing needed rebutting. (1) Mechanism. I had framed it as pre-2016 low-discount accounts stopping buying. The challenger's decomposition (q449) puts $1,080,280.56 of the $1,428,556.44, 0.7562 (q462), on entrants being more discounted per dollar than the exiters they replaced. With q451 showing the same lapse gradient among 2016-2020 onboards, the finding now describes churn across all cohorts. I kept the claim that onboarding discounts are not higher (q404, q450), which the challenger also found. (2) Money. Accepted that $1.43M is price erosion against the 2016 mix on fixed 2025 volume, not a recoverable amount. I reworded the title and conclusion and added the volume context: non-markdown list down $9,502,085.00 and exiters' list exceeding entrants' by $16,068,837.46 (q462). Valuing that needs margin data that is absent. size_query is now q462, whose decomposition_sum equals the sum of q449's components. q418's $1,428,556.45 differs only by rounding. (3) Snapshot. Added the challenger's evidence that finance prices equal ERP prices (q446), the residual is flat (q456) and lapsers matched continuers in 2016 (q436). This weakens but does not remove the concern, so it stays in could_not_tell. I also added the challenger's size, trade, branch, timing and quote-reason results as claims, with the quote evidence labelled as modest and non-causal. Confidence stays medium because the causal reason for lapses and the value of retention remain unmeasurable.

concerns: Shipped but never invoiced: 5,932 SO lines (14,244.999 units) have qty_shipped above the invoiced qty, none billed at all, steady at about 400-600 lines a year 2016-2025 (q13, q16)

Duplicate vendor bills: 1,429 bills with vendor_invoice_no '<no>-R' re-bill a PO already billed, same amount ($4,196,810.04), 963 of them paid (q52, q53); 433 unpaid older ones are all '-R' ($1,413,732.94, q63)

Vendor bills above PO: 20,194 bills' lines exceed PO value ($4,610,594.43 total, q55); 5,542 lines bill more qty than ordered, 14,869 a higher unit cost (avg 1.0549x when higher, q58); 13,949 of these bills were paid in full, $3,166,564.74 excess (q65), while 12,026 other bills were short-paid to PO value (q59, q62). Mixed handling worth understanding
Freight on bills: 21,886 bills add freight to the header (q57); 6,115 short-paid bills were paid without the freight (q59)

Customer payments are too clean: every invoice is paid exactly once in full, no partials, deductions or write-offs in ten years (q18); credit memos ($3,281,327.03) are never netted, including 6,898 invoice payments after a credit on the same order (q97)

Vendor payments always land exactly on terms (21/31/41 operating days, min = max, q60); stock POs always received exactly on expected_day in a single receipt with qty = PO (q50, q92). Likely generated/scheduled, not observed behaviour (interpretation)
Return reason codes are near-uniform across five values (1,247-1,328, q23) and credit memo reasons copy them (q24); they cannot explain returns
Opening balances are all fractional (4,548 rows, e.g. 1.742 units, q30) and drive 3,694 fractional shipped qty, mostly in 2016 (q26, q29), on items ordered in whole units (q27)
Short lines (155,280) carry ship_day = order day though nothing shipped (q9, q38)

Static costs: SO line unit_cost and PO cost equal the current product cost in every year 2016-2025 (q41, q45), while price-to-list falls from 0.8453 to 0.8232 (q44); margin trends therefore reflect price only

discontinued_on does not stop sales: 84,465 lines sold after it, incl. SKUs 'discontinued' 2015-01-01 sold through 2025 (q87, q88); 1,471 lines sold before available_from (q87). Meaning of the field is unclear

Rep table has no dates: the same 84 reps, 36 quoting every year (q68); order-taking is split almost evenly among each branch's 4 inside reps (e.g. Cleveland 31,548-31,625, q95), which looks like assignment rather than real workload (interpretation)
Customer names repeat: 340 distinct names for 6,156 customers, some 30 times across 11 branches (q43, q46); name cannot identify a customer
erp_branches.county contains city names; external tables use real counties (q84)

Service contacts: 2016 has 36,990 contacts vs 22,238 in 2017 (q74); notes are three fixed templates (q76, q78); minutes are tightly banded (q73). No notes addressed to an AI or containing instructions were found (q77, q78)
Vendor returns: 1,465 WMS return_vendor movements (2,222 units) vs 1,234 vendor credits (1,849 units), only vendors 1-4, no shared key (q64, q66)

cannot_answer: Profitability by customer, rep or branch: needs historical unit costs, freight-out, rebates, and operating expenses; costs here are a static snapshot (q41, q45)
Why returns happen: reason codes look uninformative (q23); would need inspection notes or RMA records
Whether orders were keyed correctly: no edit history or original customer document; returns 'wrong item' cannot be told apart from 'customer error' reliably (q23)
Whether a vendor bill was right: needs vendor price agreements/contracts and freight terms; only PO cost exists (q55, q58)
Lost sales from stockouts: short lines have no backorder or re-order link (q9); would need a backorder/cancel record
How customer credits were settled (refund, applied to later invoices): payments are never reduced (q97); needs the AR sub-ledger or cash application
Special-order arrival and the customer line each special PO serves: no receipt and no key (q49); needs PO-to-order link
Service contact resolution, and the order behind half the contacts (q80); needs a ticket key and outcome
Rep tenure, staffing changes and account reassignment over time: single snapshot tables; needs HR/assignment history
Why quotes were lost beyond 'price'/'job cancelled', and competitor pricing (q67)
summary_problems: cause_as_fact: "The cause is that accounts with discounts under 10% stop ordering faster"; "low-discount accounts in every cohort stop buying faster, not because accounts were repriced or new accounts signed at bigger discounts"
